notes: Identity independently verified from the supplied canonical text: title Cultural Variation in Correspondence Bias: The Critical Role of Attitude Diagnosticity of Socially Constrained Behavior; authors Yuri Miyamoto and Shinobu Kitayama; Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (2002), 83(5), 1239–1248. Printed DOI 10.1037//0022-3514.83.5.1239 corresponds to reference DOI with an extra printed slash. Primary journal article containing Study 1 methods/results, Table 1, Study 2, references and appendix, rather than an abstract or secondary excerpt. No PDF supplied; no rendering performed. Study 1/Table 1 and description Correspondence bias in WEIRD samples identify American participants, but do not distinguish real attitude versus free speech or long-persuasive versus short-unpersuasive essays. Four American proessay-versus-antiessay candidates remain: long-persuasive real attitude t(98)=6.43, p<.001; long-persuasive free speech t(98)=4.78, p<.001; short-unpersuasive real attitude t(98)=6.66, p<.001; short-unpersuasive free speech t(98)=5.81, p<.001. These are printed t statistics, not d. Table 1 prints adjusted means, original unadjusted SDs, t and p, without d. No conversion or target selection by row order/numeric matching performed. Methods report 58 American participants (29 males and 29 females) and 49 Japanese participants. American total spans diagnosticity and essay-direction conditions; Table 1 supplies no cell counts or explicit critical-test analytic N for the unresolved American contrast. Retain 58 only as a sample/contributor candidate, not extracted analytic N. No N inferred from df or summed from undocumented final groups. No explicit Study 1 participant exclusions stated in inspected methods/results. Only n_o and es_value_o assigned; all other fields/sides are unassigned placeholders. Table note evidence: Values of ts and ps are for comparisons between the proessay means and ... the antiessay means in the respective conditions.
